title: Technical Judgment at Executive Scale
description: Evaluating, making, or reversing **architecture decisions** with enough technical depth, organizational realism, and business judgment.

competency.name: Technical Judgment at Executive Scale
competency.definition: Makes high-quality technical calls by weighing architecture, team maturity, operational burden, and business consequences.
competency.whyItMatters: Senior technology leaders do not need to be the deepest specialist, but they must create the conditions for sound technical decisions and own the consequences.

prompt.primary: Tell me about a time you made or reversed a major architecture decision.
variants: Describe a time when your **technical judgment** was challenged by senior engineers.
Tell me about a time you chose a pragmatic architecture over a fashionable one.
interviewerIntent: Can the candidate reason about technical **trade-offs** beyond slogans?
Do they respect expert input without outsourcing judgment?
Can they connect architecture choices to team capability, customer impact, and business constraints?

scenario.signatureExample: A VP reopens a service-extraction decision after checkout incidents and on-call handoffs worsen, reconsolidates two unstable pieces, and keeps one service with clear ownership.
context: A portfolio-level service extraction was approved to improve team autonomy, but checkout reliability and deployment coordination got worse.
Senior engineers are split between hardening the new services, reconsolidating the unstable pieces, and waiting for teams to mature around the new boundaries.
Customers care more about payment success, recovery speed, and predictable delivery than about the target-state architecture.
constraints: Reversing the decision would delay two roadmap items and could embarrass leaders who sponsored the extraction.
Hardening every service would consume platform capacity without fixing unclear ownership.
The decision must preserve trust with senior engineers and make the learning explicit.

storyAnatomy.situation: A major service extraction, meant to accelerate teams, was causing more checkout incidents, deployment coordination, and on-call handoffs.
storyAnatomy.task: Decide whether to keep hardening the services, reverse part of the decision, or continue the migration despite the operational drag.
action: Defined reversal criteria around incident frequency, rollback time, ownership clarity, dependency age, on-call handoffs, and **payment success**.
Ran a review where service advocates, checkout leads, SRE leaders, and product leaders compared hardening, reconsolidation, and further extraction.
Stopped further extraction, reconsolidated two unstable services behind modular boundaries, and kept one service where scale and ownership justified it.
Published the reversal rationale, including the roadmap cost and what the original decision had underweighted.
result: Checkout P1/P2 incidents fell from seven in one month to two across the next two release cycles.
Median rollback time dropped from 90 minutes to 35 minutes, and cross-team on-call handoffs fell by roughly 40 percent.
Two roadmap items slipped by one month, but later extractions used explicit ownership and readiness criteria.
storyAnatomy.reflection: The lesson was that architecture direction must fit operating capability, and that reversing a stale decision is a leadership act when the evidence changes.
systemChange: Architecture decision record template with revisit triggers and rejected options.
Service extraction readiness checklist covering ownership, observability, deployment, and on-call maturity.
Regular technical **review forum** that separates reversible team-local choices from hard-to-reverse company-level architecture calls.

exampleStories.title: Constraining an ML Platform Rollout
exampleStories.promptVariant: Describe a time when your **technical judgment** was challenged by senior engineers.
exampleStories.situation: A senior engineer wanted all personalization and fraud workflows moved onto a shared ML feature platform, but fraud decisions still needed deterministic explanations, batch lineage was weak, and two recent data-quality incidents had exposed unclear feature ownership.
strongAnswerSketch: Separate workflows where shared ML features improved ranking or recommendations from workflows that required explainability, auditability, or simple rollback.
Move recommendation experiments onto the feature platform while keeping fraud blocks behind versioned rules and an explicit human-review path.
Ask the senior engineer who proposed the rollout to co-own the readiness bar for feature freshness, lineage, model rollback, and business-owner sign-off.
Measure data-quality incidents, rollback time, model-change lead time, false-positive customer impact, and support-ticket handoffs over the next release cycle.
whyItWorks: Shows domain-level technical judgment without pretending to be the deepest ML-platform expert.
Balances a senior IC's valid platform goal with explainability, operational readiness, and customer risk.
Turns a narrowed rollout into a reusable readiness mechanism for data-dependent and model-dependent systems.
exampleStories.weakVersion: I decided the ML platform was too risky for fraud, limited it to recommendations, and told the senior engineer we could revisit fraud later.
followUpAngles: Which workflows still justified the shared ML platform?
How did you preserve trust with the engineer who advocated the original design?
What data or model readiness signal changed future architecture reviews?

exampleStories.title: Modular Monolith Before Services
exampleStories.promptVariant: Tell me about a time you chose a pragmatic architecture over a fashionable one.
exampleStories.situation: Senior engineers were split between extracting microservices immediately and stabilizing a monolith that slowed teams but still had clear ownership and known failure modes.
strongAnswerSketch: Define criteria around deployment frequency, **ownership boundaries**, incident history, and team maturity.
Run a review that surfaces both camps' strongest arguments.
Choose modular boundaries first and service extraction only where ownership and scale justify it.
Invest in observability, deployment discipline, and domain ownership before distributing runtime responsibility.
whyItWorks: Uses technical criteria rather than architecture fashion.
Respects senior engineers without outsourcing judgment.
Shows sequencing, reversibility, and operating readiness.
exampleStories.weakVersion: I decided microservices were too risky and told the team to clean up the monolith first.
followUpAngles: What would have made microservices the right answer?
How did you know modularization was working?

exampleStories.title: Reversing Premature Service Extraction
exampleStories.promptVariant: Tell me about a time you made or reversed a major architecture decision.
exampleStories.situation: A portfolio-level service extraction had been approved to accelerate product teams, but after three months checkout incidents, deployment coordination, and on-call handoffs got worse while no team wanted to own the shared failure modes.
strongAnswerSketch: Reopen the decision with evidence: deployment failure rate, incident handoffs, dependency age, ownership clarity, customer-impacting latency, and on-call load.
Admit that the original extraction criteria overweighted target-state autonomy and underweighted operational readiness.
Stop further extraction, reconsolidate two unstable services behind modular boundaries, and keep one service where scale and ownership justified it.
Absorb the cost of pausing two roadmap items, publish the reversal rationale, and replace the old review with a service-readiness gate.

Show the outcome: checkout P1/P2 incidents fell from seven in one month to two over two release cycles, rollback time dropped from 90 minutes to 35 minutes, and cross-team on-call handoffs fell by roughly 40 percent.
whyItWorks: Makes a decision reversal credible by naming evidence, ownership, cost, and measured recovery.
Avoids both sunk-cost defense and blanket rejection of services.
Shows how an executive-level architecture call changes portfolio governance.
exampleStories.weakVersion: I saw that microservices were causing incidents, so I told teams to move back to the monolith and focus on delivery.
followUpAngles: What made reversal better than hardening the new services?
Who lost work or status because of the reversal?
What did the organization learn about service readiness?

exampleStories.title: Build Versus Buy for a Platform Capability
exampleStories.promptVariant: Tell me about a time you made or reversed a major architecture decision.
exampleStories.situation: A platform team wanted to build an internal workflow engine, but the company needed faster compliance readiness and lacked deep expertise in that domain.
strongAnswerSketch: Compare strategic differentiation, integration cost, vendor risk, compliance deadline, data ownership, and team opportunity cost.
Choose buy for the commodity workflow layer while building differentiating policy logic internally.
Create an exit plan around data export, integration boundaries, and owned policy logic.
Document the decision so future platform investments use the same build-versus-buy criteria.
whyItWorks: Balances technical control with business urgency.
exampleStories.weakVersion: I chose the vendor because it was faster and told the team we could replace it later if it became a problem.
followUpAngles: What vendor lock-in risk did you accept?
How did you make the decision reversible?

strongAnswerPattern.summary: The candidate shows technical reasoning, humility with experts, and pragmatic sequencing under real constraints.
moves: Frames the technical decision through constraints, options, and outcomes.
Names the criteria used to evaluate options.
Shows how dissenting technical input changed the decision or criteria.
Explains reversibility, sequencing, and operational readiness.
Names the evidence that would trigger a reversal and owns course changes without blame.
Leaves behind decision mechanisms, not just a chosen architecture.

weakAnswerPattern.summary: The candidate either defers completely to specialists or asserts authority without explaining technical **trade-offs**.
redFlags: Uses architecture buzzwords without concrete constraints.
Cannot explain what would make the decision wrong.
Frames disagreement with senior engineers as politics rather than signal.
Treats reversing a decision as embarrassment instead of learning.
Ignores operational burden, ownership, migration risk, or the cost of delay.

followUps.question: What criteria did you use to make the decision?

strong: I weighted customer impact, deployment independence, incident handoffs, ownership clarity, team on-call maturity, reversibility, and whether the choice reduced cross-team waiting.

For build versus buy, I separated strategic differentiation from commodity workflow, then scored compliance deadline, integration complexity, data ownership, vendor exit cost, and team opportunity cost.
weak: We considered reliability, scalability, and maintainability, then chose the most balanced option.
The senior engineers reviewed the options and recommended what they thought was best.

followUps.question: Which senior engineers disagreed, and what did you learn from them?

strong: The principal engineer pushing services was right that boundaries were real; I separated module boundaries from runtime distribution and asked them to co-author extraction readiness criteria.
The platform lead wanted to build because vendor lock-in was real; I accepted that risk only after defining data export, integration boundaries, and the policy logic we would keep in-house.
weak: Some engineers preferred a different architecture, but after some debate they agreed with the decision.
I let the experts argue it out and backed the option with the most support.

followUps.question: What would have told you the decision was wrong?

strong: If modularization did not reduce cross-team PR wait, incident handoffs, or release coupling within two cycles, I would reopen service extraction for the hottest boundary.
If the bought platform missed compliance dates, blocked policy changes, or failed data-export tests, the exit plan would trigger before deeper integration.
weak: If delivery did not improve, I would know we had chosen the wrong architecture.
I expected the team to tell me if the choice was not working.

followUps.question: How did future **architecture decisions** change afterward?

strong: ADRs now require rejected options, a decision owner, a revisit trigger, expected operating cost, and evidence that deployment, observability, and on-call ownership are ready.
We split architecture review into reversible team-local choices and cross-team or hard-to-reverse choices, so senior engineers could move fast without hiding company-level risk.
weak: We documented the decision and created an architecture review meeting.
I told teams to be more disciplined about trade-offs before choosing new technologies.

signals.name: Technical Depth
signals.strong: Uses concrete architecture, operational, and team constraints to explain the decision.
signals.weak: Relies on fashion, authority, or vague platform language instead of evidence.

signals.name: Expert Collaboration
signals.strong: Engages senior engineers as partners while owning the criteria and decision process.
signals.weak: Either overrules experts casually or hides behind their recommendation.

signals.name: Pragmatic Sequencing
signals.strong: Chooses a path that fits current capability, reduces near-term risk, and creates options.
signals.weak: Jumps directly to an idealized target state without sequencing the migration.

signals.name: Reversal Discipline
signals.strong: Owns stale or wrong decisions, names the evidence that changed, and adjusts course without blame.
signals.weak: Defends old decisions too long or reverses abruptly without explaining what was learned.

rubric.expected: Leads domain-level technical **trade-offs**, uses senior IC input well, and defines readiness signals before expanding a pattern.
Coordinates architecture choices across teams with explicit criteria, ownership boundaries, and migration discipline.
Balances architecture, **operating model**, talent, delivery, and business risk across a portfolio.
Sets technical direction that creates strategic leverage while managing company-level risk, capital allocation, and reversibility.

prompts.label: What technical decision was contested or high-impact?
What decision process or outcome did you own?
What criteria, experts, and trade-offs shaped the decision?
What improved, and what trade-offs remained?
What did you learn about technical judgment at your level?

relatedScenarios: Choosing build versus buy for a strategic capability.
Changing cloud, data, or AI architecture under executive pressure.
